title: Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring (Category I/II/III)
summary: The three-tier FHR classification system standardizes interpretation of intrapartum tracings and guides when to intervene versus continue observation.
key_points: Category I: normal baseline 110-160 bpm, moderate variability, no late/variable decels — reassuring, no action needed
Category III: absent variability with recurrent late/variable decels or bradycardia, OR sinusoidal pattern — predicts abnormal acid-base status
Category II is everything in between; it is the most common category and requires clinical judgment, not a fixed algorithm
Variability tiers: absent, minimal (≤5 bpm), moderate (6-25 bpm), marked (>25 bpm)
Tachysystole = >5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over a 30-minute window
Routine supplemental maternal oxygen is no longer recommended for fetal resuscitation absent maternal hypoxemia
Category III that doesn't resolve with resuscitative measures warrants expedited delivery
management: Classify the tracing using the 3-tier system every time it is reviewed
For Category II, characterize the specific abnormality and trend over time rather than reacting to a single strip
Start conservative intrauterine resuscitation first: reposition mother, IV fluid bolus, correct hypotension, reduce/stop oxytocin or uterotonics
Consider short-term tocolysis (e.g., terbutaline) for tachysystole-associated decelerations
Use amnioinfusion for recurrent variable decelerations attributed to cord compression
Reserve supplemental O2 for documented maternal hypoxemia, not as a routine fetal measure
For Category III without prompt resolution, proceed to expedited delivery
citations: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10, Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring: Interpretation and Management (current edition — verify at acog.org)

title: VBAC / Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC)
summary: TOLAC is a reasonable option for most patients with one prior low-transverse cesarean, but success and safety depend on careful candidate selection and informed counseling.
key_points: Overall TOLAC success (vaginal birth) rate is roughly 60-80% in appropriately selected candidates
Uterine rupture risk with a single prior low-transverse incision is approximately 0.5-0.9%
Absolute contraindications include prior classical or T-shaped incision, prior uterine rupture, or another contraindication to vaginal birth
Favorable candidates: one prior low-transverse cesarean, no other uterine scars, adequate pelvis, spontaneous labor onset
Validated prediction calculators can estimate an individual patient's likelihood of successful VBAC
Misoprostol for cervical ripening is avoided in patients with a prior cesarean due to increased rupture risk
TOLAC should occur where staff and resources for emergency cesarean are immediately available
management: Counsel on individualized risks/benefits using a validated VBAC success calculator; document shared decision-making
Confirm the delivering facility has immediately available anesthesia, OR, and surgical/nursing staff for emergency cesarean
Use continuous electronic fetal monitoring throughout labor
Avoid misoprostol for cervical ripening; oxytocin for induction/augmentation is acceptable with appropriate monitoring
Maintain a low threshold for emergent cesarean with signs suggestive of uterine rupture (severe pain, bradycardia/Category III, vaginal bleeding, loss of station)
Offer planned repeat cesarean as a reasonable alternative when TOLAC is declined or contraindicated
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 184, Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery (2017 — verify current edition at acog.org)

title: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) Perinatal Prophylaxis
summary: Universal late-pregnancy GBS screening with risk- and culture-based intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is the cornerstone of preventing early-onset neonatal GBS disease.
key_points: Universal vaginal-rectal culture screening is recommended at 36 0/7-37 6/7 weeks for all pregnant patients
GBS bacteriuria at any colony count during the current pregnancy is itself an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis — no need to retest
A prior infant with invasive GBS disease is an indication for prophylaxis in the current pregnancy regardless of current culture result
If GBS status is unknown at labor, give prophylaxis for risk factors: preterm labor <37 weeks, rupture of membranes ≥18 hours, or intrapartum fever
First-line agent is IV penicillin G; ampicillin is an acceptable alternative
For penicillin allergy with low anaphylaxis risk, cefazolin is preferred; for high anaphylaxis risk, use susceptibility-guided clindamycin or vancomycin
Scheduled cesarean performed without labor or ruptured membranes does not require GBS prophylaxis regardless of colonization status
management: Obtain vaginal-rectal GBS culture at 36 0/7-37 6/7 weeks unless prophylaxis is already indicated for another reason
Determine prophylaxis indication: positive culture, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, prior GBS-affected infant, or unknown status plus an intrapartum risk factor
Start penicillin G (or ampicillin) as first-line intrapartum prophylaxis, ideally with adequate time before delivery
Switch to cefazolin for penicillin allergy without high anaphylaxis risk
Use clindamycin only if susceptibility is confirmed, or vancomycin, for high anaphylaxis risk with resistant/unknown susceptibility
Skip prophylaxis for a planned cesarean with intact membranes and no labor
Communicate maternal GBS status and prophylaxis timing to the newborn care team for risk-based neonatal monitoring
citations: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 797, Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns (2020)
CDC Guidelines for the Prevention of Perinatal Group B Streptococcal Disease (verify current edition at cdc.gov)

title: Multiple Gestation: Chorionicity-Based Surveillance
summary: Chorionicity, not zygosity, determines the complication risk and surveillance intensity for twin pregnancies, with monochorionic twins requiring the closest monitoring.
key_points: Chorionicity/amnionicity should be determined as early as possible, ideally by first-trimester ultrasound (lambda vs T-sign)
Monochorionic-diamniotic (MCDA) twins are at risk for twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), TAPS, and selective fetal growth restriction
TTTS is diagnosed by oligohydramnios (deepest vertical pocket <2cm) in the donor sac plus polyhydramnios (DVP >8cm) in the recipient sac, staged by Quintero criteria I-V
Monochorionic-monoamniotic (MCMA) twins carry the highest risk (cord entanglement) and are generally managed with inpatient surveillance
Recommended uncomplicated delivery windows: dichorionic-diamniotic ~38 weeks, uncomplicated MCDA 34-37 6/7 weeks, MCMA 32-34 weeks
Antenatal fetal testing is recommended for monochorionic twins given elevated stillbirth risk relative to dichorionic twins
management: Establish chorionicity/amnionicity by ultrasound as early as possible, ideally in the first trimester
Set surveillance frequency by chorionicity: monochorionic twins roughly every 2 weeks starting around 16 weeks; dichorionic twins less frequently
Screen each monochorionic surveillance visit for TTTS using fluid/bladder criteria and stage with Quintero criteria if present
Refer significant TTTS to a fetal therapy center for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
Begin antenatal testing (NST/BPP) for monochorionic twins, often starting around 32 weeks or earlier/inpatient for MCMA
Plan delivery timing by chorionicity and any complications rather than a single fixed gestational age for all twins
Refer complicated cases (selective FGR, TAPS, MCMA) to maternal-fetal medicine or a dedicated multiples program
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Multifetal Gestations: Twin, Triplet, and Higher-Order Multifetal Pregnancies (current edition — verify at acog.org)
SMFM Consult Series, Twin Pregnancy: Surveillance and Delivery Timing (current edition — verify at smfm.org)

title: Placenta Accreta Spectrum & Third-Trimester Bleeding
summary: Prior cesarean combined with a previa or low-lying placenta is the dominant risk pattern for placenta accreta spectrum, and outcomes hinge on antenatal diagnosis plus planned delivery at an experienced center.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) risk is driven mainly by prior cesarean delivery plus placenta previa/low-lying placenta over the old scar
Ultrasound is first-line for PAS diagnosis: loss of the retroplacental clear space, placental lacunae, bridging vessels, myometrial thinning
Absence of classic ultrasound findings does not rule out PAS — clinical risk factors still matter
Placenta previa = placenta covering or within 2cm of the internal cervical os on transvaginal ultrasound after 20 weeks; many resolve by the third trimester
Classic abruption triad: vaginal bleeding, abdominal/back pain, and uterine tenderness or hypertonus; bleeding can be concealed
PAS outcomes are optimized with planned, scheduled delivery (often 34-36 weeks) at a level III/IV maternal care center, avoiding labor and placental disruption
management: Evaluate risk factors (prior cesarean, previa, prior uterine surgery) and confirm suspected PAS with targeted ultrasound by an experienced sonographer
Refer confirmed or suspected PAS to a level III/IV maternal care center for multidisciplinary planning
Plan a scheduled cesarean (often with hysterectomy, placenta left in situ) before labor onset, avoiding placental disruption
For bleeding previa: hospitalize for monitoring, avoid digital/vaginal exams, give antenatal corticosteroids if preterm, individualize delivery timing by bleeding severity
For suspected abruption: continuous fetal monitoring, assess maternal hemodynamics and coagulopathy, expedite delivery for nonreassuring status or severe abruption
Pre-arrange blood products/massive transfusion protocol and relevant surgical specialists for anticipated PAS cases
Counsel the patient preoperatively about likely hysterectomy and fertility implications when PAS is suspected
citations: ACOG-SMFM Obstetric Care Consensus No. 7, Placenta Accreta Spectrum (2018)
ACOG Practice Bulletin, Placenta Previa and Placental Abruption (current edition — verify at acog.org)

title: Antepartum Fetal Surveillance (NST/BPP/Modified BPP)
summary: Antepartum testing uses the NST, biophysical profile, or modified BPP to reduce stillbirth risk in pregnancies with maternal or fetal risk factors.
key_points: Reactive NST = at least 2 accelerations of ≥15 bpm for ≥15 seconds within 20 minutes (lower thresholds before 32 weeks)
Full BPP scores 5 components (NST, fetal breathing, movement, tone, amniotic fluid), each worth 0 or 2 points, for a max of 10
Modified BPP (NST + amniotic fluid index) is similarly predictive and less resource-intensive than the full BPP
Oligohydramnios (AFI ≤5cm or single deepest pocket <2cm) is considered abnormal independent of the rest of the BPP score
A BPP score ≤4 generally warrants prompt delivery consideration; a score of 6 is equivocal and usually repeated the same day
Testing typically starts around 32-34 weeks for most indications but earlier for more severe conditions
management: Identify the maternal/fetal risk factor driving the need for testing and the appropriate gestational age to start
Use the NST as the first-line test; if nonreactive, follow with a full or modified BPP
Score BPP components systematically and act according to the total: 8-10 reassuring, 6 equivocal/repeat, ≤4 concerning
Assess amniotic fluid volume as an independent data point, since oligohydramnios prompts further workup regardless of overall BPP score
Repeat testing weekly to twice weekly depending on the indication and its severity
Interpret results alongside growth scans, Doppler studies, and the overall clinical picture rather than in isolation
Expedite delivery for persistently abnormal or worsening surveillance, balanced against gestational age
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 229, Antepartum Fetal Surveillance (2021)

title: Cervical Insufficiency and Cerclage
summary: Cerclage type (history-, ultrasound-, or exam-indicated) is selected based on obstetric history and current cervical findings to prevent recurrent second-trimester loss or preterm birth.
key_points: Cervical insufficiency: painless cervical dilation/shortening causing recurrent second-trimester loss in the absence of labor or abruption
History-indicated (prophylactic) cerclage is placed around 12-14 weeks based on ≥1 prior second-trimester loss from painless dilation
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage is considered for cervical length <25mm before 24 weeks in a patient with a prior spontaneous preterm birth
Exam-indicated (rescue) cerclage is for cervical dilation found on exam before 24 weeks without labor, infection, or abruption
Cerclage is contraindicated with active labor, chorioamnionitis, major fetal anomaly, or significant bleeding
McDonald cerclage is the most common technique; transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed prior transvaginal cerclage
Progesterone therapy addresses a different risk pathway (prior spontaneous preterm birth) and may be used alongside or instead of cerclage
management: Take a detailed history to classify risk type: classic insufficiency history vs prior spontaneous preterm birth vs an incidental current exam finding
Place a history-indicated cerclage early (~12-14 weeks) for a classic cervical insufficiency history
For prior spontaneous preterm birth, follow serial transvaginal cervical length ultrasound from 16-24 weeks
Place an ultrasound-indicated cerclage if cervical length falls below 25mm before 24 weeks in that population
Consider exam-indicated/rescue cerclage for cervical dilation found before 24 weeks after excluding labor, infection, abruption, and anomaly
Pair with vaginal or intramuscular progesterone per indication rather than using cerclage for short cervix alone without a qualifying history
Plan cerclage removal around 36-37 weeks, or earlier for labor, rupture of membranes, or infection
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 142, Cerclage for the Management of Cervical Insufficiency (2014 — verify current edition at acog.org)
SMFM Consult Series, Cerclage for the Prevention of Preterm Birth (current edition — verify at smfm.org)

title: Obesity in Pregnancy
summary: Pre-pregnancy obesity raises risk across nearly every major obstetric complication and requires adjustments to screening timing, medication dosing, and delivery planning.
key_points: Obesity = pre-pregnancy BMI ≥30, further stratified into class I-III (class III ≥40)
Associated with increased risk of gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders/preeclampsia, macrosomia, cesarean delivery, VTE, anesthesia complications, and stillbirth
Recommended gestational weight gain is lower at higher BMI classes per national weight-gain guidelines
Early glucose screening at the first prenatal visit is recommended in obesity, in addition to standard 24-28 week screening
Medication and thromboprophylaxis dosing may need weight-based adjustment
Early anesthesia consultation is recommended for class II-III obesity to plan for airway and regional anesthesia challenges
Obesity is a recognized moderate risk factor supporting low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention, particularly with additional risk factors
management: Counsel on individualized, BMI-based gestational weight gain targets starting at the first prenatal visit
Screen for gestational diabetes early (first visit) in addition to the standard 24-28 week screen
Assess preeclampsia risk and initiate low-dose aspirin per risk-factor criteria when indicated
Arrange antepartum anesthesia consultation for class II-III obesity
Review VTE prophylaxis and other weight-based medication dosing throughout pregnancy and postpartum
Plan fetal growth assessment accordingly, recognizing ultrasound may be technically limited
Discuss delivery-related risks and logistics (positioning, incision choice, equipment needs) ahead of time, especially if cesarean is anticipated
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 230, Obesity in Pregnancy (2021)

title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Risk Assessment and Prophylaxis
summary: Pregnancy and the postpartum period markedly increase VTE risk, so structured risk assessment and risk-based prophylaxis at key clinical touchpoints are central to prevention.
key_points: Pregnancy/postpartum confers roughly a 4-5 fold increased VTE risk compared with the nonpregnant state
VTE is a leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States
Personal history of VTE is the single strongest individual risk factor; known thrombophilia is the next most significant
LMWH is the preferred agent for pharmacologic prophylaxis and treatment, both antepartum and postpartum
All cesarean deliveries should receive at least mechanical prophylaxis (sequential compression devices) if not already on pharmacologic prophylaxis
Anticoagulation timing must be coordinated around neuraxial anesthesia safety windows near delivery
Highest-risk patients (prior VTE, high-risk thrombophilia) may warrant extended postpartum prophylaxis, commonly around 6 weeks
management: Perform a structured VTE risk assessment at prenatal intake, at any antepartum admission, and again postpartum/post-cesarean
Risk-stratify patients into pharmacologic (LMWH) versus mechanical-only prophylaxis candidates
Use LMWH first-line when pharmacologic prophylaxis is indicated, timing doses around planned neuraxial anesthesia
Apply mechanical prophylaxis (SCDs) for all cesarean deliveries without pharmacologic prophylaxis and other at-risk patients
Continue or extend prophylaxis postpartum for the highest-risk patients
Evaluate acute symptoms (leg swelling/pain, dyspnea, chest pain) promptly with compression ultrasound or CTPA/V-Q as appropriate
Treat confirmed VTE with therapeutic anticoagulation and plan the transition around delivery and the postpartum period
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 196, Thromboembolism in Pregnancy (2018)
